templates.name: Principle plus case leads to consequence (S10 trade-off folded in)
Rule or timeline plus observation rejects a premise
Undercut leads to a hedged conclusion
X but not Y, so Z
Two cases or two accounts lead to a conditional or a common ground
Co-occurrence or repeated pattern leads to a link
Behaviour, design or content reveals a motive or belief (S12 example folded in)
Received view plus counterevidence leads to revision

items.subtype: T4 explanation: principle (lending rule) applied to a format
items.passage: For much of the nineteenth century, British publishers issued most new novels in three separate volumes, at prices so high that relatively few readers purchased them; readers instead borrowed novels from commercial circulating libraries, the largest of which, Mudie’s Select Library, charged a standard annual subscription that let each member borrow a single volume at a time. Mudie’s was long the format’s strongest supporter, and when it sharply cut what it would pay for three-volume sets in 1894, the format quickly disappeared. Mudie’s most likely favored the three-volume novel because the format ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: permitted the library to charge its members a separate fee for each volume they borrowed.
allowed every copy of a novel the library purchased to circulate among three members simultaneously.
made each copy of a novel less expensive for the library than a single-volume edition would have been.
gave novelists room to develop longer and more intricate plots than a single volume could hold.
items.explanation: Members of Mudie’s paid a yearly subscription that let them borrow one volume at a time. A novel split into three volumes could therefore be in the hands of three different members at once, so each copy the library bought served three times as many readers. That is a reason a lending library would favor the format, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says members paid an annual subscription, not a fee for each volume; the one-volume rule limits how much a member borrows, not how the member pays.

C.why_wrong: The text says three-volume novels were priced so high that few readers bought them; it never compares their cost to the library with that of one-volume editions.

D.why_wrong: The question is why the library favored the format. The text says nothing about plot length or what novelists wanted, and a benefit to authors would not explain the library’s interest.

sources.what: Richard Menke, ‘The End of the Three-Volume Novel System, 27 June 1894’: costly three-volume novels sustained by circulating libraries such as Mudie’s, whose subscribers borrowed one volume at a time, so one novel served three readers; in 1894 Mudie’s and W. H. Smith’s cut the price they would pay, ending the format

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature, history of the book). S2 principle plus case: one-volume borrowing rule plus three-volume format gives three simultaneous borrowers per copy. Distractors: MIX (fee per volume), CMP (cost vs one-volume edition), OUT (benefit to novelists).

fixes: 1894 corrected: Mudie’s capped what it would pay (4 shillings a volume), it did not stop paying (Menke, BRANCH essay, which supports the one-volume subscription and three readers per copy)
plainer wording (strongest supporter, that let each member borrow)
added band-6 S2 model 65502c46 (both listed models are CB medium, bands 4 and 5)

band7.why: Two steps (one-volume rule plus three volumes gives three borrowers per copy), rule two sentences before the blank; one partly-right distractor (A keeps the subscription), C and D die to one fact each, short options. Fair band 6, band 6 by plan.

items.subtype: T4 explanation: acoustic principle explains composers’ choice
items.passage: Before valves were added to brass instruments in the nineteenth century, a trumpet could produce only the pitches of the harmonic series, the limited set of notes that a tube of unchanging length naturally sounds. In the instrument’s lower register these pitches are separated by wide intervals, which is why low trumpet parts of the period consist mostly of fanfares; only in the uppermost register do the intervals become narrow. Baroque composers wrote trumpet melodies in a very high register, most likely because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: high notes carried better than low notes over the sound of a large chorus and orchestra.
fanfares, which leap between widely spaced notes, could be sounded only in that part of the instrument’s range.
the narrow intervals of the upper register made its notes easier to keep in tune than those of the lower register.
only there could the instrument sound the closely spaced notes that a melody moving by step requires.
items.explanation: Without valves, a trumpet can play only the pitches of the harmonic series. The text says these pitches are far apart low in the range and draw close together only near the top. A melody that moves from one note to the next needs closely spaced pitches, so it can be played only in that high register, which explains the composers’ choice, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The text gives no information about how well high or low notes carry over a chorus or orchestra; its explanation is the spacing of the available pitches.

B.why_wrong: The text ties fanfares, which use widely spaced notes, to the lower register, where the intervals are wide; and fanfares would not explain where composers placed their melodies.

C.why_wrong: The text does say the upper register has narrow intervals, but it says nothing about how easily any notes could be kept in tune; it links the high register to the spacing of the available pitches.

sources.what: harmonics far apart at the bottom of the series and closer together higher up; low partials give bugle-call figures; only in the extreme high (clarino) register were they close enough to play a scale

items.notes: Area: humanities (music history). S2: harmonic-series principle applied to Baroque melody writing. Distractors: CAUSE (audibility), MIX (fanfares placed in the high register), CAUSE (tuning, keeps the narrow upper intervals).

fixes: read easier than band 6: B (intervals widen) and C (valves on Baroque trumpets) each died to one stated fact; rebuilt as partly-right options: B puts fanfares and wide spacing in the high register (MIX), C keeps the narrow upper intervals but credits tuning (CAUSE); re-solved blind, D only
plainer words (limited, wide, mostly, very)
source replaced: listed page did not state the low and high spacing; wtju.net does
added band-6 S2 model 0dccbf17

band7.why: After the rebuild: two steps (narrow intervals only at the top, plus a stepwise melody needs close notes), two partly-right distractors (B, C) and one rival cause. Before the fix it read easier than band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: two principles applied to a pricing decision
items.passage: A considerable share of agricultural produce never reaches supermarkets simply because it is misshapen or blemished. Marketing researchers Siddhanth Mookerjee, Yann Cornil, and JoAndrea Hoegg found that consumers avoid such produce partly because they assume it is less flavorful and less nutritious, and that labeling it “ugly” increases purchases by making explicit that its only defect is cosmetic; consumers, however, also interpret price as an indicator of quality. Offering produce labeled “ugly” at a steep discount, rather than a moderate one, could therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: undermine the label’s effect by implying that the produce is deficient in more than appearance.
increase purchases further, since a low enough price would compensate for any lingering doubts about flavor.
lead shoppers to suspect that the attractive produce displayed nearby is overpriced.
persuade shoppers that misshapen produce is more nutritious than conventional produce.
items.explanation: According to the text, the “ugly” label works by telling shoppers that the produce’s only defect is its appearance. Because shoppers also read price as a signal of quality, a steep discount would suggest that something more than appearance is wrong with the produce, working against the message of the label. A states this consequence.

B.why_wrong: The text says shoppers treat price as a signal of quality, so a steeper discount would add to their doubts rather than compensate for them.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how shoppers judge the prices of attractive produce sold nearby.

D.why_wrong: The label conveys that the produce is no worse apart from its appearance, not that it is more nutritious than other produce, and the discount would not create that belief.

sources.what: Mookerjee, Cornil, Hoegg 2021, Journal of Marketing: ‘ugly’ label raises purchase by signaling the flaw is only aesthetic, countering inferences about taste and health; works best with moderate (20%) rather than steep (60%) discounts because a large discount signals low quality

items.notes: Area: social science (marketing). S2 with two principles (label counters quality inference; price signals quality) applied to a steep discount. Distractors: REV, CMP, EXT.

band7.why: Two principles chained (label removes the taste and health inference; price signals quality) and applied to a steep discount; B and D partly right; no aside premise or long options.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: tax rule plus supply conditions
items.passage: In the 1570s and 1580s, officials of China’s Ming dynasty consolidated the numerous taxes and compulsory labor obligations owed by households into a single annual assessment, a reform known as the Single Whip, and stipulated that this assessment be paid in silver, even though China’s domestic silver production had been declining for more than a century. Meanwhile, Spanish galleons traveling between Acapulco and Manila had begun transporting silver extracted from mines in Mexico and Bolivia across the Pacific. By requiring that taxes be paid in silver, the reform likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: reduced the quantity of silver that Chinese households needed in order to meet their obligations to the state.
encouraged Spanish authorities to open new silver mines in the Philippines to supply Chinese buyers.
helped draw silver mined on the opposite side of the Pacific into China.
led Ming officials to reopen the country’s declining silver mines rather than rely on foreign supplies.
items.explanation: The reform obliged every household to pay its taxes in silver, which raised China’s need for the metal. Because China’s own mines were in decline, that need had to be met largely from abroad, and the text notes that Spanish ships were then carrying American silver across the Pacific to Manila. So the reform likely helped draw that silver into China, as C says.

A.why_wrong: Requiring every payment in silver would increase households’ need for silver, not reduce it.

B.why_wrong: The text names Manila only as a port on the galleon route; the silver came from mines in Mexico and Bolivia, and nothing suggests mines in the Philippines.

D.why_wrong: The text says only that China’s mines had been declining; it gives no indication that officials tried to revive them.

sources.what: Single Whip reform required taxes in silver; China’s own silver mines were in decline by 1430; most silver came from foreign trade, Japan and the Americas via Manila galleons, China absorbing about half of the silver mined in Mexico and Bolivia

items.notes: Area: history (economic history). S2: silver tax plus weak domestic supply plus American silver at Manila gives silver imports. Distractors: REV, MIX (Philippine mines), CAUSE (reviving mines).

band7.why: Two steps (silver tax plus declining mines needs imports; galleons carry American silver); each distractor keeps a true piece (silver demand, the Pacific route, declining mines) but dies to one plain fact.

items.subtype: T3 prediction: timing mismatch applied to a warming climate
items.passage: Corydalis ambigua, a wildflower that blooms in the forests of northern Japan soon after the snow melts, relies for pollination chiefly on bumblebee queens that have just emerged from underground hibernation. Monitoring three populations of the plant on the island of Hokkaido for 10 to 14 years, ecologists Gaku Kudo and Takashi Ida recorded each spring when flowering began and when queens first appeared. Both events occurred earlier when snow melted early, but flowering moved earlier by much more than the queens’ emergence did. As the climate warms, increasingly early springs will therefore likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: cause the queens to emerge well before the plant’s first flowers have opened.
delay the plant’s flowering until the queens have emerged, restoring the usual timing.
allow bumblebee colonies to grow larger, since queens will have a longer season in which to forage.
reduce the plant’s seed production by leaving more of its flowers without pollinators.
items.explanation: The plant relies chiefly on bumblebee queens for pollination. When snow melts early, flowering moves forward more than the queens’ emergence does, so more flowers open before any queens are out. Flowers that go unvisited are not pollinated and set no seed, so earlier springs will likely reduce the plant’s seed production, as D says.

A.why_wrong: Because flowering advances more than emergence, early springs put flowers ahead of the queens, not the queens ahead of the flowers.

B.why_wrong: The text says flowering comes earlier, not later, when snow melts early, so nothing would restore the usual timing.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the size of bumblebee colonies or how long queens forage.

sources.what: Kudo and Ida 2013, Ecology 94: Corydalis ambigua and its bumblebee pollinators followed for 10 to 14 years in three populations; flowering onset and first overwintered queens both tracked snowmelt, but flowering ran ahead of the queens in early springs, lowering seed set

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology). S2: dependence on queens plus unequal advance of flowering and emergence, applied to warming. Distractors: REV (queens first), REV (later flowering), OUT (colony size).

fixes: source replaced: listed blog reports Kudo and Cooper 2019 (one site, 19 years), not Kudo and Ida; now the 2013 Ecology paper
method aligned with that paper: three populations, 10 to 14 years
plainer wording (soon after, moved earlier by much more)

band7.why: Three-link chain with a direction (flowering outpaces queens, flowers open unvisited, fewer seeds); A is the mismatch pointed the wrong way, a strong near miss, but C is a plain OUT and the passage runs in a straight line.

items.subtype: T4 explanation: voting rule explains a finding about campaigns
items.passage: Under ranked-choice voting, now used in a number of US cities, voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the first choice of a majority, the last-place candidate is eliminated and that candidate’s ballots are transferred to each voter’s next choice, a process repeated until one candidate has a majority. Surveying voters, political scientists Todd Donovan, Caroline Tolbert, and Kellen Gracey found that campaigns in cities using this system were perceived as less negative than those in comparable cities without it, likely because candidates in such elections ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: can win only if they are the first choice of a majority of voters before any ballots are transferred.
may need the second-choice rankings of their rivals’ supporters, whom harsh attacks could alienate.
focus their appeals on the voters who have already ranked them first rather than on other voters.
benefit when rival candidates are eliminated, since those candidates’ ballots go to them automatically.
items.explanation: When a candidate is eliminated, those ballots go to each voter’s next choice, so a candidate can win partly through other candidates’ supporters ranking them second. Attacking a rival harshly could cost a candidate those rankings. That gives candidates a reason to keep their campaigns less negative, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says that when no one is a majority’s first choice, ballots are transferred until someone has a majority, so a candidate can win without first-choice majority support.

C.why_wrong: Focusing only on voters who already rank a candidate first ignores the transferred ballots that make rivals’ supporters matter, and it would not explain less negative campaigns.

D.why_wrong: Transferred ballots go to each voter’s next choice, not automatically to any particular candidate.

sources.what: Donovan, Tolbert, Gracey 2016, Electoral Studies 42: voters in cities with preferential (ranked-choice) voting more satisfied with campaign conduct and less likely to view campaigns as negative than voters in similar plurality cities

items.notes: Area: social science (political science). S2: transfer rule plus finding of less negative campaigns gives the incentive to court rivals’ supporters. Distractors: REV and MIX misreadings of the rule.

band7.why: Two steps (transfers make rivals’ second choices matter; attacks cost them); A, C and D each misread the stated rule, so all partly right; rule two sentences before the blank; short options.

items.subtype: T2 purpose: a change in a plant reveals what it accomplishes
items.passage: Coyote tobacco (Nicotiana attenuata), a wildflower of the western United States, ordinarily opens its flowers at night and releases a fragrance that attracts hawkmoths, which feed on its nectar and pollinate it. The relationship is costly, however: female hawkmoths also deposit their eggs on the plant, and the caterpillars that hatch consume its foliage. Ecologists Danny Kessler, Celia Diezel, and Ian Baldwin found that plants attacked by these caterpillars begin producing flowers that open in the morning, when hummingbirds rather than hawkmoths are active, and that emit little of the fragrance. This change suggests that attacked plants ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: can still be pollinated while becoming less attractive to the insects whose offspring feed on them.
open their flowers in the morning mainly to conserve water that would otherwise be lost at night.
are pollinated more effectively by hummingbirds than by hawkmoths, even when no caterpillars are present.
use the scent to drive away the caterpillars that are already feeding on their leaves.
items.explanation: The text says hawkmoths both pollinate the plant and lay eggs whose caterpillars eat it. Attacked plants switch to flowers that open when hummingbirds, not hawkmoths, are active and that give off little of the scent that draws the moths. The change therefore keeps the plants pollinated while making them less attractive to the moths that would lay more eggs, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about water loss; it ties the change to caterpillar attack and to which animals visit the flowers.

C.why_wrong: The text does not compare how well the two animals pollinate, and it describes plants without caterpillars as relying on hawkmoths.

D.why_wrong: The scent attracts hawkmoths, and attacked plants produce less of it; nothing indicates that it repels caterpillars.

sources.what: Kessler, Diezel, Baldwin 2010, Current Biology, ‘Changing pollinators as a means of escaping herbivores’: Manduca-attacked Nicotiana attenuata produce morning-opening flowers with less benzyl acetone instead of night-opening, moth-attracting flowers; hummingbirds visit by day

items.notes: Area: natural science (plant ecology). S9: the plant’s change reveals its function (keeping pollination while avoiding egg-laying moths). Distractors: CAUSE (water), CMP (pollinator efficiency), MIX (scent repels caterpillars).

band7.why: Two steps (moths pollinate and lay eggs; day flowers with little scent keep pollination and avoid moths); C and D partly right, B a plain rival motive.

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: timeline of nesting rules out migration
items.passage: About 70 million years ago, the region of northern Alaska now crossed by the Colville River lay even farther north than it does today, experiencing months of continuous darkness each winter. Some paleontologists proposed that the dinosaurs whose fossils occur there were seasonal visitors that, like modern caribou, migrated southward before winter. But a team led by Patrick Druckenmiller identified bones and teeth of hatchlings and embryos from seven kinds of dinosaurs in the region’s sediments. Since these dinosaurs’ eggs would have required several months of incubation, and their hatchlings would have been too small to undertake long migrations, the team concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the dinosaurs migrated south to lay their eggs and returned north with their young each spring.
the region lay farther south 70 million years ago than it does now and so escaped long periods of winter darkness.
many of these dinosaurs likely lived in the region throughout the year rather than leaving before winter.
dinosaurs living in the region probably produced fewer young each year than did dinosaurs living farther south.
items.explanation: The young were found in the region itself, so eggs were laid and hatched there. Months of incubation would bring hatching late in the year, and the hatchlings would have been too small to travel far before winter. The dinosaurs therefore could not have left before winter as the migration idea requires; many likely stayed all year, as C says.

A.why_wrong: Remains of newly hatched and unhatched young in the region show that eggs were laid and hatched there, not farther south.

B.why_wrong: The text says the region lay even farther north than it does today and spent months in darkness each winter.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no information about how many young dinosaurs farther south produced.

sources.what: Druckenmiller et al. 2021, Current Biology: perinatal remains of seven kinds (species) of dinosaurs in the Prince Creek Formation, northern Alaska, at the highest known paleolatitude; long incubation and small hatchlings indicate nonmigratory, year-round residents; about 120 days of winter darkness

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). S3 modus tollens: if they migrated before winter they could not have nested and raised young there; young found there, so not migrants. Distractors: REV (migration kept), MIX (darkness from warmth), CMP.

fixes: ‘seven dinosaur families’ changed to ‘seven kinds of dinosaurs’: the UAF release says seven species and families could not be confirmed
plainer wording (crossed)

band7.why: S3 rejection of the migration premise, both reasons stated in the blank sentence; A rescues the old view (partly right), B and D die to one fact each.

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: dairy consumed but no lactase persistence
items.passage: Adults lacking lactase persistence, an inherited trait that keeps the body producing the enzyme that digests lactose, the principal sugar in milk, often have difficulty digesting fresh milk. Analyzing remains of herders who inhabited what is now Mongolia around 3,000 years ago, Choongwon Jeong, Christina Warinner, and colleagues detected milk proteins in the dental plaque of most individuals examined, yet none carried genetic markers of lactase persistence. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the herders acquired lactase persistence from neighboring peoples soon after they began herding.
dairy products can become a regular part of a population’s diet without that population having lactase persistence.
milk proteins preserved in dental plaque may be an unreliable indication that a person consumed dairy products.
the herders drank fresh milk more often than people in regions where lactase persistence is common.
items.explanation: The milk proteins in the herders’ dental plaque show that they consumed dairy, yet none of them carried the trait that lets adults digest lactose easily. Consuming dairy therefore did not depend on having that trait, which is what B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says none of the individuals carried markers of lactase persistence.

C.why_wrong: The text presents the milk proteins as evidence of dairy consumption and gives no reason to doubt the method.

D.why_wrong: The text does not compare the herders with any other population or say how often they drank fresh milk.

sources.what: Jeong et al. 2018, PNAS: Late Bronze Age herders in northern Mongolia (about 1300 BCE); milk proteins in dental calculus of 7 of 9 individuals; no individual showed lactase persistence

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology (archaeogenetics). S6 X but not Y: dairy eaten but no lactase persistence, so dairying did not require the trait. Distractors: REV, CAUSE (method unreliable), CMP.

band7.why: One-step X but not Y on the band-6 one-sentence model 0dba14e6; distractors contradict, doubt the method, or compare with an unmeasured group.

items.subtype: T2 revision: coins undercut a chronicle’s portrayal
items.passage: Ceolwulf II became king of Mercia in 874 after a Viking army expelled his predecessor, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, a historical record initially compiled in neighboring Wessex under Alfred the Great, characterizes him as a subservient puppet of the Vikings. But the Watlington Hoard, buried in Oxfordshire around 879, contains thirteen silver pennies on which Alfred and Ceolwulf appear enthroned together as apparent equals. These coins therefore suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Ceolwulf likely issued the pennies chiefly to persuade the Viking army that he was no longer dependent on Alfred’s support.
Alfred, rather than Ceolwulf, governed Mercia from 874 until the hoard was buried.
the Viking army that drove out Ceolwulf’s predecessor was also allied with Alfred around 879.
the Chronicle’s portrayal of Ceolwulf may reflect the interests of Alfred’s kingdom more than his actual standing.
items.explanation: Coins showing Alfred and Ceolwulf side by side as equals point to an alliance between two kings of similar standing, not to a Viking puppet. Since the Chronicle that belittles Ceolwulf was first compiled in Alfred’s own kingdom, its portrayal may say more about how Wessex wished to present events than about Ceolwulf’s real position, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The coins show the two kings together as equals, which suggests partnership with Alfred; nothing indicates that they were aimed at the Vikings or meant to show independence from Alfred.

B.why_wrong: The text says Ceolwulf became king of Mercia in 874, and the coins present him as a king beside Alfred.

C.why_wrong: The coins pair Alfred with Ceolwulf, not with the Viking army; the text says nothing of an alliance between Alfred and the Vikings.

sources.what: Watlington Hoard, buried in the late 870s; its Two Emperors pennies represent the collaboration of Alfred and Ceolwulf, while the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls Ceolwulf ‘an unwise king’s thane’ and casts him as a Viking stooge, likely Alfred’s propaganda (the Ashmolean gives 13 Two Emperors pennies)

items.notes: Area: history (early medieval England). S11: the Chronicle’s view (puppet) plus counterevidence (coins of equals) gives a revised view of the source’s reliability. Distractors: CAUSE, REV, MIX.

fixes: source replaced (Ashmolean page returns 404); The History Blog confirms the late-870s burial, Two Emperors pennies showing Alfred and Ceolwulf together, and the Chronicle’s dismissal of Ceolwulf as likely Alfred’s propaganda

band7.why: The key needs the aside ‘compiled in Wessex under Alfred’ (a band-7 trait) plus the coins, but each distractor dies to one fact (A invented motive, B contradicts 874, C swaps parties) and options are short.

items.subtype: T4 mechanism: comparison of pure and mixed plantings
items.passage: Glutinous rice, a sticky variety highly valued in China’s Yunnan Province, is especially vulnerable to rice blast, a fungal disease whose spores are dispersed by wind from plant to plant, so that a single infected plant can spread the disease throughout a field. Farmers there traditionally cultivated it in separate fields. In the late 1990s, plant pathologist Zhu Youyong and colleagues persuaded thousands of farmers instead to plant single rows of glutinous rice between rows of a hybrid variety resistant to the disease. Blast damage to glutinous rice averaged roughly 20 percent in conventional fields but only about 1 percent in the mixed fields, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: interspersing resistant plants among susceptible ones may slow blast by keeping spores from reaching other susceptible plants.
the hybrid variety protected the glutinous rice by releasing compounds into the surrounding soil that killed the blast fungus.
glutinous rice grown in mixed fields would likely produce larger harvests than the hybrid variety does.
rice blast is less likely to infect plants in Yunnan Province than plants in China’s other major rice-growing regions.
items.explanation: Blast spores travel on the wind from plant to plant. In the mixed fields, each row of glutinous rice was surrounded by resistant plants, so many spores would land on plants they could not infect instead of on another susceptible plant. That explains why damage fell from about 20 percent to about 1 percent, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The text says the spores travel by wind; it says nothing about compounds released into the soil.

C.why_wrong: The study compared blast damage to glutinous rice in two kinds of fields; it did not compare harvests of the two varieties.

D.why_wrong: The text reports results only from Yunnan and does not compare infection rates with other regions.

sources.what: Zhu et al. 2000, Nature 406, ‘Genetic diversity and disease control in rice’: Yunnan farmers interplanted blast-susceptible glutinous rice with resistant hybrid rice in 1998 and 1999; blast was 94% less severe on the susceptible rice in mixtures than in monoculture (about 20% to 1%)

items.notes: Area: natural science (plant pathology, agriculture). S1 hard: the comparison is in numbers and the key adds the wind-borne mechanism. Distractors: CAUSE, CMP, CMP (region). Key longest here.

fixes: ‘damaged 20 percent of plants’ restated as average blast damage (the paper measured severity, 94% lower in mixtures)
source replaced (UNU archive unreachable) with the Nature paper’s RePEc record

band7.why: Comparison carried by numbers, wind-borne spores three sentences before the blank supply the mechanism; B rival mechanism, C and D unsupported comparisons, so only one partly-right distractor.

items.subtype: T1 conditional: opposite outcomes for two kinds of book
items.passage: Analyzing sales of more than 200 books reviewed in the New York Times, marketing researchers Jonah Berger, Alan Sorensen, and Scott Rasmussen found that negative reviews were followed by declining sales when the book’s author was already well established. For books by relatively unknown authors, however, negative reviews were followed by increased sales. In subsequent experiments, a negative review heightened participants’ awareness of an unfamiliar book, and this awareness persisted after their unfavorable impression of the book had faded. These findings suggest that the effect of a negative review on a book’s sales ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: is likely determined largely by how harshly the reviewer criticizes the book.
is greater for books by well-known authors than for books by unfamiliar ones, though sales decline in both cases.
can be favorable or unfavorable, depending on how familiar potential readers already are with the author.
lasts longer for unfamiliar books than for familiar ones because readers quickly forget unfamiliar titles.
items.explanation: The same kind of review lowered sales for books by well-known authors and raised them for books by little-known authors. The experiments suggest why: for an unfamiliar book, the review mainly made readers aware of it. Whether a negative review helps or hurts therefore depends on how familiar readers already are with the author, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text compares books by known and unknown authors; it says nothing about how harsh the reviews were.

B.why_wrong: The text says sales rose after negative reviews of books by little-known authors, so sales did not decline in both cases.

D.why_wrong: The experiments found that awareness of the unfamiliar book persisted; nothing says readers quickly forget unfamiliar titles, and the text does not compare how long the effects last.

sources.what: Berger, Sorensen, Rasmussen 2010, Marketing Science 29(5): negative New York Times reviews hurt sales of books by established authors but increased sales of books by relatively unknown authors; experiments show negative publicity raises awareness, and for unknown books the negative impression fades while awareness remains; more than 200 books

items.notes: Area: social science (marketing). S7 two cases with opposite outcomes give a conditional; the distinguishing feature is the author’s familiarity. Distractors: VAR (harshness), REV (both decline), MIX (forgetting).

band7.why: S7 two cases to a conditional, which the band-7 report keeps at band 6; B (half the evidence reversed) and D (mechanism garbled) partly right.

items.subtype: T1 revision: letters overturn an attribution
items.passage: When Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl was published in 1861, its title page named only its editor, the white abolitionist author Lydia Maria Child, and the narrator was identified only by the pseudonym “Linda Brent.” Many scholars therefore long regarded the book as a novel by Child. During the 1980s, however, historian Jean Fagan Yellin located correspondence in which Harriet Jacobs, who had escaped enslavement in North Carolina, explained that she had written the book and adopted a pseudonym to avoid detection. This correspondence suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the book is better understood as Jacobs’s account of her own life than as a novel by Child.
Child wrote most of the book herself, drawing on lengthy interviews she had conducted with Jacobs.
Jacobs used a pseudonym so that readers would believe Child had written the book.
the book reached a much wider audience in the nineteenth century than scholars had assumed.
items.explanation: Scholars had treated the book as Child’s novel because only her name appeared on it. Jacobs’s letters show that she wrote it and used a pseudonym to protect herself, so the book is best read as her own account, not as Child’s fiction, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The letters show that Jacobs wrote the book; the text gives Child the role of editor, not author, and mentions no interviews.

C.why_wrong: The text says Jacobs used a pseudonym to avoid detection, not to make readers credit Child.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how widely the book was read.

sources.what: before Jean Fagan Yellin’s work the accepted view (e.g. John Blassingame) was that Incidents was a fictional novel by Lydia Maria Child; Yellin used Jacobs’s letters to establish Jacobs as the author; her edition appeared in 1987

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature). S11: received view (a novel by Child) plus counterevidence (Jacobs’s letters) gives the revision. Distractors: MIX (authorship), MIX (motive), OUT.

fixes: source replaced: listed NC page does not say scholars took the book for a novel by Child; the Yellin article does (accepted view before Yellin, her 1987 edition)

items.subtype: T1 revision: survey of records changes a view of diet
items.passage: Crocodiles, alligators, and their relatives have long been regarded as strict carnivores, and when fruit turned up in their stomachs, researchers generally assumed that it had been swallowed accidentally, perhaps while the animals were seizing prey. Reviewing published records from around the world, zoologist Steven Platt and colleagues found that 13 of the 18 crocodilian species for which dietary information exists have been documented consuming fruit, from dozens of plant families. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: crocodilians probably eat fruit mainly when their usual prey becomes scarce.
most crocodilian species obtain more of their nutrition from plants than from animals.
eating fruit may be a more regular part of crocodilians’ diets than researchers once assumed.
crocodilian species that eat fruit are more closely related to one another than to other species.
items.explanation: Researchers had dismissed fruit in crocodilian stomachs as an accident. Platt’s team found fruit eating recorded in most crocodilian species with dietary data and across many kinds of plants, which suggests that fruit is a more regular part of their diets than once thought, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about when crocodilians eat fruit or about the availability of prey.

B.why_wrong: Showing that most species eat some fruit does not show that plants supply most of their nutrition.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how the species are related to one another.

sources.what: Platt et al. 2013, Journal of Zoology: frugivory recorded in 13 of 18 crocodilian species with dietary data; plants from 34 families and 46 genera; fruit had often been treated as accidental ingestion

items.notes: Area: natural science (zoology). S11: received view (strict carnivores, fruit accidental) plus counterevidence gives the revision. Distractors: CAUSE, EXT, OUT.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: record-keeping device applied to a fraud
items.passage: In medieval England, the royal treasury, known as the Exchequer, documented payments on tally sticks. A clerk carved notches of various sizes across a wooden stick to represent the sum deposited and then split the stick lengthwise, so that identical notches appeared on both halves. The individual who had paid preserved one half, called the stock, while the Exchequer preserved the other, called the foil. Because no two sticks split identically, the halves of each stick fit together only with each other. Anyone who afterward carved additional notches into a stock to exaggerate a payment would therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: need to request a replacement stick from the Exchequer before presenting the altered stock.
be exposed as soon as the stock was set beside the foil that the Exchequer had kept.
find that the added notches appeared on the Exchequer’s foil as well.
succeed in the deception, since the stock was the only record of the payment that existed.
items.explanation: The notches were cut before the stick was split, so the stock and the foil carried the same notches. Notches carved into the stock later would appear on the stock alone, and the mismatch would be plain when the two halves were put together, as B says.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says a payer had to request a replacement stick; the question is what would happen once the altered stock was checked.

C.why_wrong: Notches carved after the split would appear only on the stock, not on the foil kept by the Exchequer.

D.why_wrong: The Exchequer kept the foil, a second record of the payment, so the stock was not the only record.

sources.what: Science Museum: tally stick split, lender kept the stock and debtor the foil with the same information; halves fitted together perfectly so tampering with the notches could be detected by reuniting stock and foil

items.notes: Area: history (medieval administration). S2: matching halves plus a later alteration gives detection. Distractors: OUT, REV, REV.

items.subtype: T5 status of evidence: a later context undercuts a claim
items.passage: While excavating Katsuren Castle on the Japanese island of Okinawa, archaeologists unearthed several copper coins that X-ray analysis indicated had been minted in the Roman Empire during the fourth century. The castle, however, was occupied from approximately the twelfth to the fifteenth century, an era when Okinawa traded extensively with China and Southeast Asia, and the same site also yielded an Ottoman coin from the seventeenth century. Therefore, the Roman coins ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: were most likely brought to Okinawa by traders from the Roman Empire during the fourth century.
show that Katsuren Castle was built several centuries earlier than archaeologists had believed.
were probably the main currency used by the castle’s inhabitants in their trade with China.
do not by themselves show that people from the Roman Empire ever traveled to Okinawa.
items.explanation: The coins were made in the fourth century but were found at a castle occupied about a thousand years later, during a period of wide trade, and alongside a much later Ottoman coin. They could have reached Okinawa long after they were minted, passed along trade routes through China or Southeast Asia. So they do not, on their own, show that people from the Roman Empire came to Okinawa, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The coins were found in a castle occupied centuries later; nothing shows they arrived in the fourth century or with Roman traders.

B.why_wrong: The coins’ age shows when they were minted, not when the castle was built; the text gives the castle’s period of use as the twelfth to fifteenth centuries.

C.why_wrong: The text says only that a few Roman coins were found; it says nothing about the castle’s currency.

sources.what: Roman coins (about 300 to 400 CE) and Ottoman coins (1687) found at Katsuren Castle, Okinawa, in 2016; castle occupied from the 12th to 15th centuries during thriving trade with China and Southeast Asia; no direct Roman ties thought to have existed

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. S5 undercut: an object’s later context allows a rival route, so the claim is not established. Distractors: EXT, MIX, OUT.

fixes: one Ottoman coin (1687), not coins, as every report gives it
plainer wording (traded extensively)

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: natural experiment in ballot order
items.passage: Political scientists have long suspected that candidates listed first on a ballot gain votes simply because of their position, but the effect is difficult to measure where names appear in a fixed order. California offers an unusual opportunity. Since 1975, the state has used a randomly ordered alphabet, drawn before each election, to arrange the candidates in its first assembly district and has then rotated that order across the remaining districts, so that each candidate appears first in some districts and lower in others. Comparing candidates’ vote shares across districts, Daniel Ho and Kosuke Imai found that in primary elections candidates received more votes where they were listed first, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: candidates in general elections benefit from appearing first on the ballot more than candidates in primaries do.
voters in districts that rotate the order of candidates are more likely to vote than voters in other districts.
the position of a candidate’s name on the ballot can influence some voters’ choices.
arranging candidates’ names in alphabetical order would remove any advantage of appearing first.
items.explanation: Because California’s rotation puts each candidate first in some districts and lower in others, comparing the same candidate’s results across districts isolates the effect of position. Candidates did better where they were listed first, so ballot position can influence some voters’ choices, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text reports results for primary elections only; it gives no evidence that the effect is larger in general elections.

B.why_wrong: The study compared vote shares, not turnout, and every California district uses the rotated order.

D.why_wrong: Any fixed order, including an alphabetical one, still lists some candidate first, and the study did not test alphabetical ordering.

sources.what: Ho and Imai 2008, Public Opinion Quarterly: California randomized alphabet since 1975, rotated across assembly districts; in primaries being listed first benefits candidates; general-election effects mainly for minor-party candidates

items.notes: Area: social science (political science). S1: the rotation makes position the only varied factor; outcome differs, so position matters. Distractors: CMP, VAR, EXT.

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: anatomy of a fossil settles which trait came first
items.passage: Bats are the only mammals capable of powered flight, and most species also navigate by echolocation, emitting calls and interpreting the returning echoes. Echolocating bats possess an enlarged cochlea, the structure of the inner ear that processes sound. Nancy Simmons and colleagues have described Onychonycteris finneyi, a 52-million-year-old bat from Wyoming whose limb bones indicate that it could fly but whose cochlea is small, like those of fruit bats that do not echolocate. The researchers therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: flight probably evolved in bats before echolocation did.
O. finneyi relied on echolocation to hunt but on eyesight to navigate.
modern fruit bats descended directly from O. finneyi.
the cochlea of bats has likely become smaller over the past 52 million years.
items.explanation: An enlarged cochlea goes with echolocation, and O. finneyi had a small cochlea, so it probably could not echolocate. Yet its limb bones show that it could fly. An early bat that flew without echolocating suggests that flight came first in bats, as A says.

B.why_wrong: A small cochlea like those of bats that do not echolocate indicates that O. finneyi probably did not echolocate at all.

C.why_wrong: A shared trait, a small cochlea, does not show direct descent, and the text says nothing about ancestry.

D.why_wrong: Most bats today echolocate and have enlarged cochleas, so the evidence points to the cochlea becoming larger, not smaller.

sources.what: Simmons et al. 2008, Nature: Onychonycteris finneyi, 52 million years old, Green River Formation, Wyoming; could fly, but small cochlea like non-echolocating fruit bats indicates no echolocation; flight evolved before echolocation

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). S3: if echolocation came first, an early flying bat would show an enlarged cochlea; it does not, so flight came first. Distractors: REV, EXT, REV.

items.subtype: T1 link: pollution levels and errors go together
items.passage: Fine particulate matter—airborne particles small enough to pass from the lungs into the bloodstream—is a well-documented threat to physical health, but its cognitive consequences are more difficult to isolate. Economists Steffen Künn, Juan Palacios, and Nico Pestel installed air-quality sensors in the venues of German chess tournaments over several seasons and used a chess engine to evaluate every move the players made. When indoor concentrations of fine particles were elevated, players were more likely to commit errors, and their errors were more severe, particularly when the players were under time pressure. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: chess players who train in clean air are less affected by pollution during tournaments than other players are.
time pressure may cause chess players to breathe more rapidly and therefore to inhale more particles.
air quality in rooms where tournaments are held is generally worse than air quality outdoors.
even indoor levels of particulate pollution may impair the quality of people’s decisions.
items.explanation: The study found that players made more and larger errors on days when indoor fine-particle levels were higher. The errors were judged move by move, so the link is to the quality of the players’ decisions. That suggests that particulate pollution indoors may impair decision making, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about where players trained or how training conditions affected them.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about breathing; it reports only that the effect of particles was larger under time pressure.

C.why_wrong: The sensors measured indoor air only, so the text gives no basis for comparing indoor and outdoor air.

sources.what: Künn, Palacios, Pestel, Indoor Air Quality and Strategic Decision-Making (Management Science): sensors in German chess tournament venues; higher indoor PM2.5 raised the probability and size of errors evaluated by a chess engine, most under time pressure

items.notes: Area: social science (economics). S8: two measures rise and fall together, so they are linked. Distractors: CMP, CAUSE, CMP.

items.subtype: T2 purpose: an artist’s action reveals her aim
items.passage: In 1969, artist Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a manifesto calling for “maintenance art,” arguing that the repetitive labor of cleaning and caring that keeps households and cities functioning is seldom considered worthy of attention. A decade later, as the unsalaried artist-in-residence of New York City’s Department of Sanitation, she began Touch Sanitation, an eleven-month performance. In it, she traveled to every sanitation district in the city and shook hands with each of the department’s roughly 8,500 workers, telling each one, “Thank you for keeping New York City alive.” With these handshakes, Ukeles most likely intended to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: persuade city officials to raise the wages paid to the city’s sanitation workers.
give personal recognition to people whose work she believed was usually overlooked.
recruit sanitation workers to perform in her future works of maintenance art.
show that the department’s artist-in-residence should receive a salary for her work.
items.explanation: Ukeles’s manifesto argued that maintenance work rarely gets attention. Shaking the hand of every sanitation worker and thanking each one in person was a way of giving that attention to the people who do such work. So her aim was most likely to recognize workers whose labor usually goes unnoticed, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about wages; the handshakes and the thanks address recognition, not pay.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that Ukeles asked the workers to take part in future performances.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions that her position was unpaid, but nothing connects the handshakes to her own pay.

sources.what: Ukeles, Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969; unsalaried artist-in-residence at the NYC Department of Sanitation from 1977; Touch Sanitation (1979 to 1980), shook hands with about 8,500 sanitation workers saying ‘Thank you for keeping New York City alive’

items.notes: Area: humanities (visual and performance art). S9: action plus stated aims reveal the purpose. Distractors: CAUSE (wages), OUT (recruiting), ECHO (unpaid post).

items.subtype: T4 reason: an animal’s behavior and an experiment reveal its purpose
items.passage: Caterpillars of the silver-spotted skipper, a North American butterfly, live in shelters that they construct by folding over part of a leaf. Biologist Martha Weiss discovered that these caterpillars don’t simply drop their waste, called frass, near the shelter. Instead, they fling it far away. When Weiss put frass on leaves next to some caterpillars, predatory wasps killed far more of those caterpillars than of caterpillars on leaves with glass beads. The caterpillars most likely fling their frass because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: frass left inside the shelter would make the folded leaf too heavy to stay closed.
the frass marks a path that helps them find their way back to the shelter.
frass near a shelter can help predators find the caterpillar inside it.
wasps feed on frass when they cannot find any caterpillars to eat.
items.explanation: When Weiss put frass near caterpillars, wasps found and killed many more of them than when beads were placed there instead. So frass near a shelter helps predators find the caterpillar, which explains why the caterpillars throw it far away, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the weight of frass or the leaf.

B.why_wrong: The caterpillars throw their frass away from the shelter, and the experiment ties frass to predators, not to finding the way back.

D.why_wrong: The wasps killed caterpillars near frass; nothing suggests that wasps eat frass.

sources.what: Weiss 2003, Ecology Letters, ‘Good housekeeping: why do shelter-dwelling caterpillars fling their frass?’: silver-spotted skipper caterpillars fling frass; wasps killed 14 of 17 caterpillars on leaves with frass vs 3 of 17 with glass beads

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). S9: behavior plus experiment reveal the reason. Distractors: OUT, REV, MIX.

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: comparison of label types
items.passage: Many people say they want to eat more vegetables, but cafeterias often have a hard time getting diners to pick them. Psychologists Bradley Turnwald, Danielle Boles, and Alia Crum tested whether the names given to vegetable dishes make a difference. In a large university dining hall, the same vegetable dishes were served each day under one of four kinds of labels: plain labels, two kinds of labels about health, and labels that made the dishes sound delicious, such as “twisted citrus-glazed carrots.” More diners chose the vegetables on days when they had the delicious-sounding labels than on other days. This finding suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: diners like carrots better than other vegetables when the carrots are glazed.
labels that focus on health are the best way to get diners to eat vegetables.
people who eat in dining halls eat more vegetables than people who eat at home.
describing vegetables in appealing ways may lead more people to choose them.
items.explanation: The dishes themselves stayed the same; only the labels changed. Because more diners chose the vegetables when the labels made them sound delicious, the way vegetables are described can affect whether people choose them, as D says.

A.why_wrong: Glazed carrots appear only as an example of a label; the study did not compare carrots with other vegetables.

B.why_wrong: The delicious-sounding labels, not the health labels, drew the most diners.

C.why_wrong: The study took place only in a dining hall and says nothing about eating at home.

sources.what: Turnwald, Boles, Crum 2017, JAMA Internal Medicine: Stanford dining hall, four label types (basic, healthy restrictive, healthy positive, indulgent) on the same vegetables; indulgent labels chosen 25% more than basic and 41% more than healthy restrictive

items.notes: Area: social science (psychology). S1: only the label varied, outcome differed. Distractors: ECHO, REV, CMP.

fixes: ‘four kinds of labels’ listed only three; now plain, two kinds about health, and delicious (as in the study)
option B wording matched (‘focus on health’)

items.subtype: T1 conclusion: animal remains show a past condition
items.passage: Today the Ténéré region of Niger is one of the driest parts of the Sahara Desert, and almost no rain falls there. In 2000, a team led by paleontologist Paul Sereno discovered an ancient cemetery there called Gobero, where people lived at different times between about 10,000 and 4,500 years ago. Along with about 200 human graves, the team found the remains of large fish and crocodiles, animals that cannot survive without water available throughout the year. These discoveries suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the people buried at Gobero traveled to faraway coasts to catch fish.
the area around Gobero once had a lake or other water that lasted all year.
the Sahara was once wetter than any other region of Africa.
crocodiles were once able to survive in the desert without any water.
items.explanation: Large fish and crocodiles need water all year, yet their remains were found at Gobero, in a place that is now desert. So when people lived at Gobero, the area must have had lasting water, such as a lake, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text gives no sign that the people traveled to coasts, and crocodile bones are not explained by fishing trips.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about other regions of Africa.

D.why_wrong: The text says these animals cannot survive without water that lasts all year.

sources.what: Gobero, Ténéré desert, Niger; found by Paul Sereno’s team in 2000, excavated 2005 to 2006; about 200 graves with remains of large fish and crocodiles from the green Sahara, when the area bordered a large lake

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. S3: animals need permanent water; their bones are there; so the area once had permanent water. Distractors: CAUSE, CMP, REV.

fixes: occupation given as ‘at different times between’ 10,000 and 4,500 years ago: the sources describe two populations separated by a dry period

items.subtype: T1 link: colors in paintings track eruptions
items.passage: When a large volcano erupts, it can send ash and gases high into the atmosphere, where they spread throughout the world. For a few years, these particles scatter sunlight in a way that can make sunsets look much redder than usual. Atmospheric scientist Christos Zerefos and his colleagues calculated how much red and green there was in more than 500 paintings of sunsets made between 1500 and 1900. Sunsets painted within three years of a significant eruption, such as that of Tambora in 1815, were typically redder than other sunsets. This finding suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: some old paintings may record what the sky actually looked like when they were made.
after 1815, painters chose to paint sunsets more often than they painted other scenes.
volcanic eruptions happened more often before 1900 than they have since then.
painters used redder paints after major eruptions because new kinds of paint became available.
items.explanation: Ash and gases from large eruptions make real sunsets redder for a few years. Sunsets painted in the years after major eruptions also had more red in them. This suggests that the painters were showing the redder skies they saw, so some old paintings may record how the sky really looked, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The study measured colors in sunset paintings; it did not count how often painters chose sunsets over other subjects.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how often eruptions happen today.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no information about new paints; it links the redder sunsets to particles from eruptions.

sources.what: Zerefos et al. 2007, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics: red-to-green ratios in 554 sunset paintings (1500 to 1900) correlate with volcanic aerosols; paintings made within three years of major eruptions such as Tambora (1815) are redder

items.notes: Area: humanities and natural science (art and atmosphere). S8: redder painted sunsets follow eruptions, so paintings may record the atmosphere. Distractors: OUT, CMP, CAUSE.
